components.note: ⺮ is the bamboo-like top part; as it appears in 笑 it is a visual part and not about plants.
夭 (a bent, youthful figure) forms the lower part, which together suggest a crinkled, bent-over face.

example.english: He spoke to me with a smile.
example.fact: 笑 covers both a smile and a laugh; the difference is made with extra words, such as 微笑 (smile) and 大笑 (laugh loudly). It is also the verb for laughing at someone: 笑话 means a joke or to ridicule, so context matters.

components.note: 辶 (walking) suggests going through options and picking one.
先 (xiān) gives a rough sound hint; the vowels are related.

example.fact: 选 is a verb for picking among options and forms 选择 (to choose; a choice), 选手 (contestant) and 选举 (election). It is often used with a resultative: 选好了 ('have chosen'), 选中 ('have picked out').

components.note: 辶 (walking) fits the idea of distance travelled.
元 (yuán) gives the sound almost exactly; the tone is different only.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jiā lí xuéxiào hěn yuǎn.
example.english: My home is far from school.
example.fact: To say 'far from', Chinese uses 离 before the place and 远 after: 离这儿很远. Its opposite is 近 (jìn, near). It can also mean 'by far' in comparison patterns: 远比…好 ('far better than').

components.note: Simplified from 兒, which pictured a child with a large head and soft skull; the modern form keeps only a pair of legs.

example.fact: 儿 is most often seen as the suffix in northern speech, such as 花儿 and 玩儿, where it gives a rhotic 'r' sound to the syllable. As a word on its own, it means child or son, as in 儿子 and 儿童 (children).

components.note: 疒 (sickness) shows illness, here of the mind.
风 (fēng) gives the sound exactly.

example.english: He seems to have gone crazy.
example.fact: 疯 can be literal (疯子, a madman) but is also very colloquial for intense enthusiasm: 疯狂 (crazy, frenzied), 玩疯了 ('played like crazy') and 疯了 (as in 'I'm going nuts!').

components.note: 扌 (hand) shows the physical act of swapping.
奂 (huàn) gives the sound exactly.

example.fact: 换 means to replace one thing with another, not to alter it: 换衣服 (change clothes), 换钱 (exchange money), 换车 (change trains). For 'to change' in the sense of becoming different, Chinese uses 变 instead.

components.note: 犭 (dog) is a leftover animal radical, probably chosen for the idea of suspicious sniffing.
青 (qīng) gives a rough sound hint; the final is similar.

example.pinyin: Nǐ cāi wǒ zài xiǎng shénme?
example.fact: 猜 is the usual verb for guessing: 猜谜 (guess a riddle), 猜对了 (guessed right) and 猜测 (to speculate). In the game 猜拳 (rock-paper-scissors) it means to play a guessing hand game.

components.note: 广 (a building) is the frame that houses furniture.
木 (wood) shows the material the bed is made of.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng tǎng zài chuáng shang.
example.english: I want to lie on the bed.
example.fact: 床 uses the measure word 张 (一张床) and doubles up as a measure for bedding, like 一床被子 (a quilt). It forms compounds like 起床 (get up), 床单 (bed sheet) and 病床 (hospital bed).

components.note: 冂 (a frame, like a boundary) represents the enclosure.
人 (person) sits inside the frame, giving the idea of being inside.

example.fact: 内 is a formal word for 'inside' and 'within', as in 国内 (domestic), 内容 (content), 内心 (inner heart) and 一周内 (within a week). Its opposite is 外 (wài, outside).

components.note: 殳 (a hand with a tool) shows a striking or splitting action, cutting something into pieces.
The left part is the thing being cut, so the character reads as 'a piece cut off'.

example.pinyin: Zhè duàn lù hěn nán zǒu.
example.english: This stretch of road is hard to walk.
example.fact: 段 is both a noun and a measure word for portions: 一段时间 (a period of time), 一段话 (a passage of speech) and 段落 (paragraph). It is also a surname.

components.note: 人 (person, here a roof-like shape) sits on top as the one giving the order.

example.fact: 令 is a literary causative verb, most often seen in the pattern 令人 + adjective ('to make one feel…'), such as 令人高兴 and 令人失望. It also means 'an order' in 命令 and 口令 (password, command), and is an honorific prefix in 令尊.

components.note: 氵 (water) marks a liquid.
酉 (a fermenting jar) is the container for wine, and it also gives the sound.

example.fact: 酒 is the general word for any alcoholic drink, not only wine: 白酒 (baijiu), 啤酒 (beer), 红酒 (red wine). In compounds like 酒店 it means 'hotel' in Chinese, though 'wine shop' is its original sense.

components.note: A simplified form of 發; the original showed a bow being let loose, but the simplified shape does not break into clear parts.

example.pinyin: Tā gěi wǒ fāle yì tiáo xiāoxi.
example.fact: 发 has a huge range: 发短信 (send a text), 发烧 (have a fever), 发财 (get rich), 发现 (discover) and 出发 (set off). As a separate character 发 (fà) means hair, as in 头发, which is the same simplified character with a different reading.

components.note: 欠 (a yawning mouth) shows breath and voice.
哥 (gē) gives the sound exactly; it was once written twice (哥哥) in older forms.

example.fact: 歌 takes the measure word 首 (一首歌), and the verb is 唱: 唱歌 (to sing). It forms 歌手 (singer), 歌曲 (song) and 儿歌 (children's song).

components.note: 口 (mouth) shows that singing uses the mouth.
昌 (chāng) gives the sound; the finals are the same, and the initial is related.

example.fact: 唱 is the verb for singing and for performing opera, as in 唱京剧. It also means to call out, as in 唱名 and, in slang, 唱反调 (to take the opposite stance).

components.note: 冖 (a roof) shows the building where learning happens.
子 (child) is the learner, the one being taught.

example.fact: 学 is a verb ('to learn') and also a suffix for fields: 数学 (math), 科学 (science), 大学 (university), 学生 (student). 学 and 习 combine as 学习 (to study), the usual way to say 'study'.

components.note: 车 (cart) shows that this counts vehicles.
两 (liǎng) gives the sound; the tones differ only by one step.

example.english: There is a car at the door.
example.fact: 辆 is the measure word for vehicles with wheels: 一辆车, 一辆自行车 (bicycle), 一辆公共汽车 (bus). For airplanes and boats, Chinese uses different words (架, 艘).

components.note: 扌 (hand) shows reaching out to feel.

example.english: I am going to visit a friend.
example.fact: 探 describes reaching out to find something: 探索 (explore), 探险 (adventure), 探望 (visit someone ill) and 探头 (stick one's head out). In daily speech it is more often seen inside compounds than on its own.

components.note: 彳 (step) shows movement toward a place.
寺 (temple or court) is the place where one waits to be received.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng zài jiā dāi yì tiān.
example.english: I want to stay home for a day.
example.fact: 待 has two main readings: dāi ('to stay', colloquial, as in 待在家) and dài ('to treat, to wait', as in 对待, 等待, 招待). The 'stay' sense is often written 呆 in casual writing, so both forms appear online.

components.note: 亻 (person) shows a person falling.
到 (dào) gives a loose sound hint; the finals are the same.

example.fact: 倒 has two readings: dǎo ('to fall, to collapse', as in 摔倒) and dào ('to pour, upside down', as in 倒水). Many learners need the context to pick the right reading: 倒了 (fell) vs. 倒茶 (pour tea).

components.note: Simplified from 離, in which a bird is caught in a net; the modern shape no longer breaks into clear parts, so learn it as a whole.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jiā lí xuéxiào hěn jìn.
example.english: My home is close to school.
example.fact: 离 is the word for distance: A 离 B 很远 / 很近 means A is far from or near to B. It also means to leave or separate, as in 离开 (leave) and 离婚 (divorce), and is used in 离不开 (can't do without).

components.note: 彳 (step) shows movement.
王 (wáng) is a visual part on the right and gives the sound; wáng and wǎng differ only in tone.

example.fact: 往 is a preposition meaning 'towards' and is used with directions: 往左 (to the left), 往前 (forward), 往南 (south). It also forms 往往 ('often, frequently') and 以往 (in the past).

components.note: Simplified from 萬, which was a picture of a scorpion; the modern form is just a horizontal stroke with a hooked piece below.

example.pinyin: Zhèlǐ yǒu yí wàn gè rén.
example.english: There are ten thousand people here.
example.fact: 万 is the unit of ten thousand, which makes Chinese big numbers different from English: 十万 is 'one hundred thousand', 一百万 is 'a million'. It also means 'extremely' in 万分 and 万一 ('in case').

components.note: 氵 (water) suggests branching streams, which is the original sense of 'a branch' or 'a faction'.

example.english: The company is sending him to Beijing.
example.fact: 派 is a verb for assigning or dispatching someone, as in 派人 and 派出所 (local police station). It also means a faction, school or style, as in 学派, 党派 and 派对 (party, borrowed from English).

components.note: Simplified from 關, which showed a door with a bar across it; the modern form is much reduced and does not break into clear parts.

example.fact: 关 means to close or turn off: 关门, 关灯 (turn off the light), 关机 (shut down). It also means a customs checkpoint (海关) and is the word in 关系 (relationship) and 关心 (care about).

components.note: 勹 (a wrapping shape) encloses the words.
口 (mouth) inside it means spoken words, so the character reads as a unit of speech.

example.fact: 句 is both the word for a sentence and its measure word: 一句话 (one sentence), 句子 (sentence), 句号 (period). Note that the ‘gōu’ reading of this character is a rare variant.

components.note: 二 (two lines for heaven and earth) frames the character.
The crossing strokes between them show the five elements or the number five; the earliest forms were simply a cross of two strokes.

example.fact: 五 is also in 五一 (May 1st, Labour Day) and in classical lists like 五行 (the five elements). It is also used for 'several' loosely, as in 五花八门 ('all kinds of').

components.note: 非 (two things back to back) shows leaning against something.
告 (gào) gives the sound; the finals are very close.

example.fact: 靠 means to lean on or depend on: 靠窗 (by the window), 靠自己 (rely on oneself), 靠谱 (reliable, colloquial). It also means to be near to, as in 靠近.

components.note: 屮 (a sprout) shows a young plant.
土 (earth) is the soil it grows from, so the character means growth and birth.

example.fact: 生 is one of the most versatile characters: 学生 (student), 生日 (birthday), 生活 (life), 生气 (angry), 生病 (to get sick) and 生菜 (lettuce). It means 'raw' or 'unfamiliar' as in 生字 (new character).

components.note: Looks like 田 (field) with a stroke running through it; the original picture is debated and the shape is best learned as a whole.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì yóu wǒ lái zuò.
example.fact: 由 is a formal preposition meaning 'by' or 'from': 由你决定 ('it's up to you'), 由北向南 (from north to south). It also forms 理由 (reason), 自由 (freedom) and 由于 (because of).

components.note: 田 (field) shows farmland.
力 (strength) is the labour put into it, so the character means a man who works the land.

example.fact: 男 is a bound form seen in 男人 (man), 男孩 (boy), 男朋友 (boyfriend) and on restroom signs. The character shows a field (田) and strength (力), reflecting the old idea that men worked the fields.

components.note: 女 (woman) is the left side.
口 (mouth) on the right; together they were read as a woman following instructions, giving the sense of 'according to, as'.

example.hanzi: 如果明天下雨，我们不去。
example.pinyin: Rúguǒ míngtiān xiàyǔ, wǒmen bú qù.
example.english: If it rains tomorrow, we won't go.
example.fact: 如 on its own is literary ('like', 'as'), but it's the core of many common words: 如果 (if), 比如 (for example), 如何 (how) and 不如 (not as good as).

components.note: 扌 (hand) shows that pointing is done by hand.
旨 (zhǐ) gives the sound exactly and adds the sense of 'purpose' or 'direction'.

example.english: He talks while pointing at the map.
example.fact: 指 is both 'finger' (手指) and the verb 'to point'. It is also used in 指的是 ('what is meant is'), 指导 (to guide) and 指南 (guide, as in a handbook).

components.note: 夂 (a foot coming down) shows someone arriving.
卜 (a small stick) stands for a marker; together they suggest standing at a place.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen yǒu hěn duō xiāngtóng zhī chù.
example.english: We have many things in common.
example.fact: 处 has two readings: chù ('place, aspect', as in 好处 'benefit', 到处 'everywhere') and chǔ ('to deal with, to be in', as in 处理). Here it appears as a noun for places and aspects.

components.note: 门 (door) frames the character.
日 (sun) shines through the gap of the door, showing a space between.

example.pinyin: Zhè liǎng gè rén zhījiān yǒu wùhuì.
example.english: There is a misunderstanding between these two.
example.fact: 间 is also the measure word for rooms: 一间房 (a room). It is also found in 时间 (time), 空间 (space), 中间 (middle), 房间 (room) and 之间 (between).

components.note: 米 (rice) shows the grain left over after brewing.
曹 (cáo) gives a loose sound hint; the final is similar.

example.fact: 糟 is mostly used in 糟糕 (terrible, how awful) and 乱七八糟 (a complete mess). The original sense is the dregs of fermented grain, as in 酒糟.

components.note: 亻 (person) shows that this is about a person's act.
俞 (yú) gives the sound; the initial differs but it is the same family.

example.pinyin: Yǒu rén tōule wǒ de qiánbāo.
example.fact: 偷 also means 'secretly': 偷看 (peek), 偷听 (eavesdrop) and 偷懒 (slack off). The thief is 小偷, and 偷东西 is the phrase for 'to steal things'.

components.note: 丷 (horns or hair) sits on top of the head.
自 (nose, here standing for the face) forms the lower part, giving a picture of a head.

example.pinyin: Zhè shì yì shǒu hǎotīng de gē.
example.fact: 首 is the measure word for songs and poems (一首歌, 一首诗), and its basic meaning is 'head' or 'first': 首都 (capital), 首先 (first of all), 首次 (first time).

components.note: 口 (mouth) shows a vocal sound.
合 (hé) gives a loose sound hint.

example.fact: 哈 is an onomatopoeic character for laughter, written as 哈哈 for 'haha'. It also appears in 哈欠 (yawn), and in transliterations of names like 哈佛 (Harvard).

components.note: 酉 (wine jar) is here for the idea of sobering up from drink.
星 (xīng) gives the sound; the initial and final are close.

example.pinyin: Wǒ zǎoshang liù diǎn xǐng le.
example.english: I woke up at six in the morning.
example.fact: 醒 is often used as a result complement: 睡醒 (wake up from sleep) and 叫醒 (wake someone up). It also means to sober up (酒醒) and to become aware (觉醒, 提醒 'to remind').

components.note: 八 (to divide) shows the splitting action.
刀 (knife) is the tool that cuts.

example.fact: 分 is highly versatile: a minute (五分钟), a point in a score (三分), a cent (一分钱) and the verb 'to divide'. In 分数 (score) and 十分 (very), the reading and use differ.

components.note: 咅 (bù) gives the sound exactly.
阝 (a city or place) shows an administrative region.

example.fact: 部 is a measure word for films, books and works (一部电影), and a noun for departments and ministries (外交部, 部门). It also means 'a part', in 部分 (part) and 全部 (all).

components.note: 凡 (all, common) frames the character.
口 (mouth) inside shows many mouths agreeing in speech.

example.fact: 同 appears in 同学 (classmate), 同事 (coworker), 同意 (agree), 不同 (different), 一同 (together). It also acts as a preposition 'with', as in 同…一起.

components.note: 丷 (a divider) marks the split.
牛 (ox) shows a thing divided in half.

example.english: It is half past three now.
example.fact: 半 comes after the number and measure word: 三点半 (3:30), 一个半小时 (one and a half hours). In 半夜 and 半路 it means 'in the middle of'.

components.note: Four dots standing for small grains or sand; the idea of 'few' is built from the character for small, 小, with a stroke taken away.

example.fact: 少 has two readings: shǎo ('few', as here) and shào ('young', as in 少年). Its opposite is 多 (duō, many), and 少 + verb pattern: 少吃点 means 'eat a bit less'.

components.note: 扌 (hand) shows the physical act of carrying.
是 (shì) gives a rough sound hint; the finals are close.

example.fact: 提 literally means to carry something by hand (提包), and extends to 'to raise' in 提高 (improve), 提出 (put forward) and 提醒 (remind). It's also the character in 提前 (in advance).

components.note: 斤 (axe) is the right side and suggests chopping or splitting; the left part 其 is a basket shape, and the link to 'this' is a later borrowing.

example.fact: 斯 mostly appears in transliterating foreign names, such as 斯坦福 (Stanford) and 莫斯科 (Moscow). In classical Chinese, it also means 'this'.

excludeSuggestion: Mainly occurs in transliterated names (斯坦福, 莫斯科) and literary text; rarely a standalone word.

components.note: 力 (strength) shows that it involves effort.
八 (bā) gives a loose sound hint; the sound link is loose.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì wǒ lái bàn.
example.fact: 办 is the practical verb for getting things done: 办事 (run errands), 办公室 (office) and 办法 (method), as in 没办法 ('no way'). It also means to set up or run, as in 办学校 or 办婚礼.

components.note: 攵 (a hand holding a stick) shows the teacher's authority.
孝 (xiào) gives the sound, with the same final.

example.fact: 教 has two readings: jiāo (the verb 'to teach', as here) and jiào (noun, as in 教育 'education' and 宗教 'religion'). The double-object pattern 教 + person + subject (教我中文) is typical.

components.note: 力 (strength) shows effort being added.
口 (mouth) shows words of encouragement, so adding strength with words.

example.fact: 加 is the verb 'to add' and the plus sign, and it's also used in 加油 ('add oil', 'go for it!'), 加班 (work overtime) and 加入 (join). 加油 is also the word for filling up a car.
